358.title: Indra returns: the dreamer isn't the self either (8.9–8.10)
358.hook: halfway home, Indra sees the flaw: if the reflection is the self, it goes blind with the body; so he walks back, firewood in hand
358.tomorrow: Indra returns again: not even deep sleep
358.howItsDone: Students in many Hindu traditions return to their teacher with questions again and again; carrying firewood (samit-pani) is the traditional sign of approaching a teacher as a student.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Prajapati, and both Indra and Virochana mistake the reflection in a pan of water for the self. Your line was the reflection isn't you. Did a mirror remind you of the one looking? Week five of year two begins. Day three hundred fifty-eight.
screen: `PRAJAPATI — THE REFLECTION ISN'T YOU.`

segments.voice: A conversation ends, and it went well. Then, about a block later, it hits. Wait. That doesn't make sense. The words replay, the hole gets bigger, and the walking stops. Now there's a choice: keep going and let it go, or turn around, go back, and admit it didn't land. Indra, king of the gods, has just left his teacher content, and now he is standing on that sidewalk, halfway home.
screen: `FEELING GREAT, THEN A BLOCK LATER.` → `WAIT. THAT DOESN'T MAKE SENSE.` → `KEEP WALKING, OR TURN AROUND?`

segments.voice: On the road, before he reaches the gods, Indra thinks it through. If the self is that reflection, then when the body is well dressed, it's well dressed. When the body is blind, it's blind. When the body is lame, it's lame. When the body dies, it dies. I see nothing good in this. So he turns around. He walks back to Prajapati with firewood in his hands, the sign of a student asking to be taught. Prajapati says: you left content. Why are you back? Indra tells him. And Prajapati answers: it is so. I'll explain it further. Live here another thirty-two years. The king of the gods signs up for thirty-two more years because one answer didn't hold. When the years are up, Prajapati gives the next teaching: the one who moves about happily in dreams, that is the self. Better, surely. The dreamer isn't blind when the body is blind, isn't lame when the body is lame. Indra leaves, content again. And again, on the road, the doubt comes. Yes, the dreamer isn't harmed by the body's faults. But in dreams, it's as if someone is killing him, chasing him. It's as if he feels pain. He even weeps, as it were. I see nothing good in this either. And so, once more, he turns around. Notice the pattern. Prajapati doesn't give the whole answer at once. He gives an answer good enough to test, and waits for the student to find its edge. The teaching isn't only in the answers. It's in Indra's willingness to walk back.
screen: `IF THE BODY IS BLIND, SO IS IT.` · `BACK, WITH FIREWOOD IN HAND.` · `THE DREAMER: SURELY THIS ONE?` · `BUT IN DREAMS, HE WEEPS.` · then, large: `NOT THE DREAM.`

segments.voice: Today's practice watches the inner movie. Sit and settle. Close your eyes. Notice the pictures that start on their own: a memory, a plan, an image, a little scene. Like a dream, but awake. Don't follow them. Just notice: a picture is showing, and something is aware of it. When a scene pulls you in, notice that too, and step back. Not the dream. The one aware of the dream. The bell holds the time.
Indra returns. The king of the gods walks back to his teacher, twice, because the reflection and then the dreamer didn't hold up.
screen: `INDRA RETURNS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: not the dream. Today, when a worry plays like a movie in your head, notice that you're the one watching it. Day three hundred fifty-eight.

359.title: Indra returns again: not even deep sleep (8.11–8.12)
359.hook: deep, dreamless sleep seems like the answer, until Indra notices that nobody is home there; after a hundred and one years, Prajapati finally says it
359.carry: the one who sees through the eye
359.tomorrow: the horse sacrifice as the cosmos
359.howItsDone: Many Vedanta teachers end their teaching of the Chandogya with Prajapati's instruction to Indra, and the inquiry into the seer behind the senses is central to Hindu contemplative practice, including the modern self-inquiry taught by Ramana Maharshi.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Indra returns, because the dreamer, chased and weeping, wasn't the self either. Your line was not the dream. Did you watch a worry like a movie? Day three hundred fifty-nine.
screen: `INDRA RETURNS — NOT THE DREAM.`

segments.voice: The best sleep of your life. No alarm, no dreams, nothing at all, and you wake up feeling completely new. Ask anyone where they were during those hours, and they'll say: nowhere. I was out. And yet something got you safely from night to morning. Indra has now spent sixty-four years with his teacher. The reflection wasn't the self. The dreamer wasn't the self. So Prajapati tries the deepest rest there is.
screen: `NO ALARM, NO DREAMS.` → `WHERE WERE YOU? NOWHERE.` → `SIXTY-FOUR YEARS SO FAR.`

segments.voice: After another thirty-two years, Prajapati says: when someone is fast asleep, completely at peace, and knows no dream, that is the self. Immortal, fearless. That is Brahman. Indra leaves content, and on the road, the doubt comes a third time. In deep sleep, he doesn't know himself as I am this. He doesn't know these beings. It's as if he's been wiped out. I see nothing good in this. And back he goes. This time, Prajapati says: live here five more years. Add them up: thirty-two, thirty-two, thirty-two, and five. A hundred and one years. And then, finally, Prajapati speaks plainly. This body is mortal, gripped by death. But it's the dwelling of a self that is deathless and has no body. While you're tied to the body, pleasure and pain hold you. But pleasure and pain don't touch what has no body. Then he gives the line our carry comes from. When the eye looks out into space, the one who is there is the person in the eye. The eye is just for seeing. The one who knows, let me smell this, is the self; the nose is for smelling. The one who knows, let me speak, is the self; speech is for speaking. Let me hear: the ear is for hearing. Let me think: the mind is its divine eye. Look at the journey. Not the reflection, which is seen. Not the dreamer, who suffers. Not deep sleep, where nobody's home. The self is the one who sees through the eye, hears through the ear, thinks through the mind. You never see it, because it's always the one seeing.
screen: `DEEP SLEEP: NOBODY HOME.` · `A HUNDRED AND ONE YEARS.` · `THE BODY IS MORTAL; IT IS NOT.` · `THE EYE IS FOR SEEING.` · then, large: `THE ONE WHO SEES THROUGH THE EYE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice rests as the one who sees. Sit and settle, eyes open, softly. Look at something in front of you. Notice: the eye is for seeing. And there's the one who sees. Listen to a sound. The ear is for hearing. And there's the one who hears. Notice a thought. The mind is for thinking. And there's the one aware of it. Don't try to find that one. Just rest as it, seeing, hearing, knowing. The bell holds the time.
Indra returns again. Not the reflection, not the dreamer, not deep sleep. After a hundred and one years: the self is the one who sees through the eye.
screen: `INDRA RETURNS AGAIN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the one who sees through the eye. Today, three times, look at something and remember the one who is seeing it. Day three hundred fifty-nine.

360.title: The horse sacrifice as the cosmos (1.1)
360.hook: the Brihadaranyaka, the great forest teaching, opens by turning a king's horse sacrifice into the whole universe: the dawn is its head
360.tomorrow: in the beginning there was nothing
360.howItsDone: The ashvamedha is rarely if ever performed today, but the Brihadaranyaka is studied in Vedic schools of the White Yajur Veda and by Vedanta students, and its opening is often read as a meditation on the world as one sacred body.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-SIXTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Indra returns again, a hundred and one years, and the self is the one who sees through the eye. That closed the Chandogya. Did you remember the one seeing? Today a new Upanishad begins. Day three hundred sixty.
screen: `INDRA RETURNS AGAIN — THE ONE WHO SEES THROUGH THE EYE.`

segments.voice: A king's horse, turned loose under guard. That's how tradition describes the start of the ashvamedha, the royal horse sacrifice. The horse wandered, the accounts say, for a year, and the lands it crossed were claimed for the king unless someone fought to stop it. Then came the sacrifice itself. And it's with this horse that the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad begins. Not with the ritual's rules, though, or its costs. With a vision.
screen: `THE KING'S HORSE, FREE FOR A YEAR.` → `WHEREVER IT WALKS, THE KING CLAIMS.` → `NOT RULES. A VISION.`

segments.voice: Its first words, in Sanskrit, are usha va ashvasya medhyasya shirah. The dawn is the head of the sacrificial horse. Then it keeps going, part by part. The sun is its eye. The wind is its breath. The universal fire is its open mouth. The year is its body. The sky is its back, the air between earth and sky its belly. The stars are its bones, the clouds its flesh, the rivers its entrails, the plants and trees its hair. When it yawns, that's lightning. When it shakes itself, thunder. When it makes water, rain. And its neighing is speech. Read slowly, it's a portrait of the whole world, drawn in the shape of one animal. You've seen this move before. The Chandogya took the priest's song and found om inside it. Now the Brihadaranyaka takes a king's great ritual and says: look up. The real horse is already here. Dawn breaks across its head every morning. Its breath is the wind on your face. Some teachers take the passage this way: as a meditation that lets anyone, not only a king, take part in the sacrifice by seeing the world as it. Brihadaranyaka means the great forest teaching. It belongs to the White Yajur Veda, and it was taught, tradition says, in the forest, away from the village. Over the coming weeks it will bring us to Yajnavalkya, and to the philosopher Gargi. But it starts here: at sunrise, with a horse the size of the sky.
screen: `USHA VA ASHVASYA MEDHYASYA SHIRAH.` · `SUN ITS EYE, WIND ITS BREATH.` · `THE REAL HORSE IS ALREADY HERE.` · `THE GREAT FOREST TEACHING.` · then, large: `THE DAWN IS ITS HEAD.`

segments.voice: Today's practice sees the horse. Sit and settle. Picture the sky at dawn, the first light along the horizon: its head. Feel the air on your skin: its breath. Think of the clouds: its flesh. Rivers you know: running through it. Trees outside: its hair. Breathe slowly, and let the whole world feel like one living body, with you somewhere inside it. The bell holds the time.
Ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice. The Brihadaranyaka opens by seeing the sacrificial horse as the universe: the dawn its head, the sun its eye, the wind its breath.

361.title: In the beginning there was nothing; death covered it (1.2)
361.hook: a second creation story, stranger than Uddalaka's: at first there was nothing here at all, covered by death, which is hunger
361.tomorrow: the gods and demons and the breath
361.howItsDone: Hindu scriptures contain many creation accounts, from the Rig Veda's hymns to the Upanishads and Puranas, and teachers generally present them side by side as different windows rather than as a single official version.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: ashvamedha, the opening of the Brihadaranyaka. Your line was the dawn is its head. Did you catch the first light? Day three hundred sixty-one.
screen: `ASHVAMEDHA — THE DAWN IS ITS HEAD.`

segments.voice: Twenty days ago, Uddalaka told his son: in the beginning there was Being alone, and it thought, let me be many. Calm, almost serene. Now open the Brihadaranyaka to its second section, and you get a very different first sentence. In the beginning there was nothing here at all. All this was covered by death. And death, it says, is hunger. Two great Upanishads, two creation stories. Hindu tradition has kept them both, side by side.
screen: `BEING ALONE, CALM AND SERENE.` → `NOW: NOTHING, COVERED BY DEATH.` → `TWO STORIES, KEPT SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: In Sanskrit it begins: naiveha kimcanagra asit. Nothing at all was here in the beginning. Mrityunaivedam avritam asit, ashanayaya. This was covered by death, by hunger. Ashanaya hi mrityuh: for hunger is death. Then death does something. It makes a mind, thinking: let me have a self. It moves about, chanting praise, and from its praise water arises. The froth on the water hardens into the earth. Death toils, and from its heat, fire is born. Then it wants a second self, and through the mind, it joins with speech. The seed becomes the year. Before that, the text says, there was no year. When the year is born, death opens its mouth to swallow it, and the newborn cries out, bhan! That cry becomes speech. Death thinks: if I eat this, I'll have less food. So instead, through speech, it brings forth everything: the verses of the Vedas, the rituals, people, animals. And whatever it brings forth, it begins to eat. Then death longs to offer a greater sacrifice. It toils, and its body swells, and the text plays on a word: the swollen one, ashva, the horse. There's yesterday's horse, back again. What does it mean that the world comes from hunger? One way to hear it: everything alive wants. Eats, reaches, grows, consumes. The text looks straight at that and says it goes all the way down, to the first stirring of anything at all. Hunger isn't an accident in the world. In this story, it's where the world came from.
screen: `NOTHING HERE, COVERED BY DEATH.` · `FOR HUNGER IS DEATH.` · `THE NEWBORN YEAR CRIES OUT: BHAN!` · `THE SWOLLEN ONE: THE HORSE.` · then, large: `FROM HUNGER, THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Today's practice watches hunger without obeying it. Sit and settle. Notice any wanting in you right now: for food, for your phone, for the sit to end, for something to happen. Don't act on it. Don't push it away. Just watch it, the way you'd watch weather. Notice how it rises, leans forward, and sometimes fades on its own. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Ashanaya, hunger. The Brihadaranyaka's creation: nothing, covered by death, which is hunger, and from that hunger, mind, water, earth, fire, speech and the world.
screen: `ASHANAYA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: from hunger, the world. Today, notice one want as it rises, and let it pass once without feeding it. Day three hundred sixty-one.

362.title: The gods and demons and the breath (1.3)
362.hook: the gods audition every sense to sing their victory chant, and only the plain breath can't be corrupted
362.tomorrow: "I am" — the self alone, afraid, then desiring
362.howItsDone: Many Hindus chant asato ma sad gamaya at the start of study, worship or a gathering, and teachers often explain its three lines as the movement from death to the deathless.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, ashanaya: in the beginning there was nothing, and death covered it. Your line was from hunger, the world. What did your own hunger build yesterday? Day three hundred sixty-two.
screen: `FROM HUNGER, THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Lead me from the unreal to the real. From darkness to light. From death to the deathless. It's chanted in Sanskrit before classes, pujas, yoga sessions, school assemblies. And it comes from today's chapter of the Brihadaranyaka, at the end of a strange little war story. The gods and the demons, both children of the creator Prajapati, are fighting over the worlds. The gods have a plan: win with a chant. All they need is a singer the demons can't corrupt. So they start auditioning the parts of the body.
screen: `LEAD ME FROM THE UNREAL TO THE REAL.` → `WHERE DOES IT COME FROM?` → `THE GODS NEED A SINGER.`

segments.voice: First they ask speech. Speech sings for them, but keeps the best part for itself: the pleasure of speaking well. The demons notice, rush at it, and pierce it with evil. That, says the text, is why we say things we shouldn't. Then smell. Then the eye. Then the ear. Then the mind. Each one sings, each one keeps something back, each one gets pierced. That's why we see, hear and think things we wish we hadn't. Last, the gods turn to the breath in the mouth, the plain breath that keeps you alive. Breath sings. The demons rush at it too, and they shatter, the text says, like a clod of earth thrown against a stone. Why breath? One common reading: it took nothing for itself. It sang for everyone. A few weeks ago, the Chandogya told this same battle in a few lines, and its longer story had breath win by threatening to leave. Here the Brihadaranyaka tells the battle in full, and on this reading breath wins because it's the one faculty that doesn't grab. Then breath carries each of the others past death. Speech becomes fire. The eye becomes the sun. The ear becomes the directions. The mind becomes the moon. And the chapter ends with the chant: asato ma sad gamaya, tamaso ma jyotir gamaya, mrityor ma amritam gamaya. The text explains its own words. The unreal is death; the real is the deathless. Darkness is death; light is the deathless. So this chant is, in its home, a prayer to be carried the way breath carries the senses.
screen: `SPEECH SINGS, AND KEEPS SOME FOR ITSELF.` · `EYE, EAR, MIND: EACH ONE PIERCED.` · `THE DEMONS SHATTER ON THE BREATH.` · `ASATO MA SAD GAMAYA.` · then, large: `BREATH IS UNTOUCHED BY EVIL.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the one who sang. Sit, and let the breath move without steering it. Notice how it takes nothing for itself: it comes in, feeds every part of you, and goes. When a thought grabs you, a sound, a worry, a plan, let it be, and come back to the breath under it. If you pray, you can say the old chant silently on the out-breath: from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to the deathless. The bell holds the time.
Prana, breath, the life-force. In this story prana is the one faculty the demons couldn't pierce, because it sang for everyone and kept nothing back.
screen: `PRANA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: breath is untouched by evil. Today, when you catch yourself about to say something you'll wish you hadn't, give it one breath first. Day three hundred sixty-two.

363.title: "I am" — the self alone, afraid, then desiring (1.4)
363.hook: before anything else exists, the self says its first words, then feels its first fear, then its first loneliness
363.tomorrow: the self split in two — husband and wife, the whole world
363.howItsDone: Students of the Upanishads read this passage as part of the Brihadaranyaka's creation account; in Vedanta teaching it is often paired with aham brahma asmi, I am Brahman, from the same chapter (1.4.10), one of the great sayings.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gods auditioned every sense to sing, and only prana, the plain breath, couldn't be pierced. Your line was breath is untouched by evil. Did one breath stop one sentence? Day three hundred sixty-three.
screen: `BREATH IS UNTOUCHED BY EVIL.`

segments.voice: A knock on a door. Someone inside calls: who is it? And the answer often comes before any name: it's me. A small habit, easy to miss. The Brihadaranyaka stops to explain it, in the middle of telling how the world began. That habit, it says, goes all the way back to the first moment there was anyone at all. Today, the first words ever spoken, and the two feelings that came right after them.
screen: `WHO IS IT?` → `IT'S ME.` → `THE FIRST WORDS EVER SPOKEN.`

segments.voice: Chapter one, section four. In the beginning, the text says, there was only the self, in the shape of a person. It looked around and saw nothing but itself. And the first thing it said was aham asmi. I am. So it came to be called I. That's why, the text adds, when anyone is called even now, they first say it's me, and then say whatever other name they have. Then something happened. The self was afraid. That's why, the text says, a person alone is afraid. And then it thought: there's nothing here but me. What am I afraid of? And the fear left. Because, the text says, fear only comes from a second. Then the self had no joy. That's why a person alone has no joy. And it wanted a second. Three moods in a few lines: I am, then fear, then longing. Notice which one thinking can cure. Fear goes the moment the self sees there's nothing else to fear. Loneliness doesn't go that way. It turns into wanting, and the wanting, tomorrow, becomes a whole world. Later Hindu philosophy uses this same little word, aham, in two very different ways. Ahamkara, the I-maker, is the ego that says me, mine, my name. And in Advaita Vedanta, the phrase aham brahma asmi, I am Brahman, from a few lines later in this same chapter, points at an I with no name tacked on after it. The first words in this story come before either reading: just I am, before any other name arrives.

364.title: The self split in two — husband and wife, the whole world (1.4)
364.hook: the lonely self makes itself fall in two, and the two halves chase each other through every kind of creature
364.tomorrow: the self is dearer than a son
364.howItsDone: Students read this as part of the Brihadaranyaka's creation account in chapter one; in many Hindu weddings the couple is spoken of as two halves of one, and the wife is called ardhangini, the half of the body.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the self alone said its first words, aham asmi, I am. Then it was afraid, then it was lonely, and it wanted a second. Did you hear yourself say it's me? Day three hundred sixty-four.
screen: `AHAM ASMI.`

segments.voice: People still say it at weddings: my other half. It sounds like a greeting card. Here it is in the Brihadaranyaka, one of the oldest Upanishads, and it isn't a greeting card at all. It's a creation story. Yesterday the self was alone, afraid, then lonely. Fear went away when it thought clearly. Loneliness didn't. The self wanted a second, and there was no second anywhere. So it did the only thing it could. It used itself.
screen: `MY OTHER HALF.` → `ALONE, AND NOTHING ELSE ANYWHERE.` → `IT USED ITSELF.`

segments.voice: The self, the text says, was as big as a man and a woman holding each other. It made itself fall in two. And from that came husband and wife. The Sanskrit plays on its own words here: the verb for fall is pat, and husband and wife are pati and patni. The text then quotes the sage Yajnavalkya, whom we'll meet properly in two days: each of us, he used to say, is like half of something split. Translators argue over the exact object, half a shell or half a split pea, but the picture is the same. You are the half, and the empty space beside you is the shape of the other. The two halves joined, and humans were born. Then the story turns strange and wide. She thinks: he made me from himself, how can he join with me? I'll hide. She becomes a cow. He becomes a bull. She becomes a mare; he, a stallion. A she-goat, a goat. A ewe, a ram. And on and on, the text says, down to the ants. Every pair of creatures in the world comes out of that chase. And at the end the self knows: I am this whole creation, because I poured it out of myself. So the story is about a marriage, and about much more than a marriage. Everything that comes in twos, wanting and wanted, is the one self looking for itself. Look back at this week. Indra learned the dreamer isn't the self, then not even deep sleep. The horse became the cosmos. Death's hunger made a world. Breath stayed clean. I am. And today, the half.

segments.voice: Two minutes with the other half. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who completes something in you: a partner, a friend, a sibling, a child, someone gone. Notice the shape they leave beside you, the space only they fill. Don't fix anything or say anything. Just let the space be there, and let it be full. If no one comes to mind, rest in the line itself, and notice how much of the world comes in pairs. The bell holds the time.
Ardha, half. In the Brihadaranyaka, the one self falls into two, and every pair of creatures comes from that split; each of us, Yajnavalkya says, is ardha, half of something split.
